demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
He is a 20-year-old South Asian man who walks into the session with a worn leather notebook tucked under his arm. He says he is a writer-aspiring, mostly. He works as a junior content writer at a small marketing firm in the city, but he tells me he hasn't written anything of his own in months. The notebook is full of blank pages. He looks at it sometimes, like he expects the words to appear on their own.

He came to therapy at his mother's insistence, after she found him sitting on the bathroom floor at two in the morning, shaking. He says he doesn't remember much of that night. But he remembers the night before, and every night before that for the past seven months.

The traumatic event happened last winter. His cousin-three years older, almost like a brother-died in a motorcycle accident. It was a routine ride, a short trip to buy groceries. A truck ran a red light. The cousin was gone before the ambulance arrived. He got the call at four in the afternoon while he was working on a draft for a blog post. He says he heard the words, then he heard his own voice telling his boss he needed to leave, and then he was outside in the parking lot, not remembering how he got there.

That first week was a blur. The funeral, the rituals, the relatives he had never met before. He says he felt numb, like he was watching everything through a window. He didn't cry until three weeks later, when he was alone in his room, looking at a photo of them laughing at a family wedding. Then the crying wouldn't stop. He started sleeping less, then barely sleeping at all. He started seeing his cousin's face in quiet moments-while brushing his teeth, while waiting for the train. Once, he was crossing the street and thought he saw him in a passing car. He stopped walking. A stranger pulled him by his arm just before a taxi sped past.

At work, he struggles to concentrate. His editor has commented on his declining quality, the way his sentences have become shorter, more clipped. He used to write long, flowing paragraphs about everyday life. Now he can only write in fragments. He avoids writing about loss, about death, about anything that might lead him back to that afternoon. But the fragments still come: a line about a red light, a note about a helmet left on a shelf. He deletes them immediately.

He is haunted by the moment he heard the news. The sound of his uncle's voice, cracking. The smell of the office coffee. The exact time on his laptop screen-4:17. He tells me that whenever he looks at a digital clock and sees 4:17, his heart starts pounding. He feels like he is back in that parking lot, standing alone, the asphalt hot under his feet. He has started avoiding looking at clocks. He turned his phone face down at his desk. He took the battery out of his bedside alarm.

Physically, he feels on edge all the time. He snaps at his colleagues for small things. He can't sit through a meeting without needing to leave. When his mother touches his shoulder unexpectedly, he flinches. He has lost his appetite. Food tastes bland, like cardboard. He drinks black tea but doesn't taste it.

He tries not to think about his cousin, but the memory intrudes anyway-in dreams, in daydreams, in the silence between traffic lights. He sees the accident from his cousin's perspective, even though he wasn't there. He imagines the impact, the sound. Sometimes he imagines that he was in the car instead, that it was his own body that hit the pavement. He feels guilty for living, for being here, for writing meaningless marketing copy while his cousin rots in the ground.

His PCL-5 score of 72 tells me what I already sense: this is severe, pervasive, unrelenting. He feels disconnected from other people, even from himself. When he looks in the mirror, he doesn't recognize the face staring back. It looks like a stranger who happens to wear his clothes, carry his notebook, walk his path home.

He hasn't written a single personal piece since the accident. He holds the notebook in his lap during our sessions. Sometimes his thumb traces the spine. But the pages stay blank.
